title: Leroy Cooper, the underrated baritone and lead saxophonist
summary: Cooper later directed Ray Charles' band; Fields praises his willingness to play whatever dance music the crowd wanted.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: You had Leroy Cooper, the great baritone man who went on to be with Ray Charles.
Yes, he went on to be Ray Charles' band director.
with him, but he wasn't the leader when I was in the band. Edgar Willis was. But we had a great rapport.

Really, Leroy Cooper was one of my favorites among the sax that I did have, because he was just--why I lasted as long as I did, all along I would try to play for people. Now I liked when I had a musician if he was way out that was all right, but we're not going to do that all night, and I would try and look over the crowd; I would even have my book before I met the crowd to get all elements. So Leroy looked like he was a youngster but he could catch on to what I was meaning.
Yeah, that's it. I remember we had a formal dance coming up and I knew they were going to want this dance, put your little foot; so I got to talking with some of the guys and they said oh,
Some of the guys said it was corny?

Yeah. Leroy said if that's what they want, let's get it. That's the way Leroy was and I don't remember exactly, but I think Leroy was in the band about three years when he was inducted in the service, World War II, out of my band.
I think Leroy Cooper is one of the least recognized lead saxophone players; I think he's the most underrated saxophonist that I've ever known.
